commenti.body:
Great analysis. Ambition, contentedness, and one's reach exceeding one's grasp are running through lines in the movie, and we can see them all from a different perspective in each of the four main characters.

Colm is the most explicitly ambitious, and though he's certainly musically talented, as you said he's not the savant he aspires to be, and rather than accept that he blames Padriac to avoid confronting the fact of his own inadequacy. 

Siobhan, too, is too ambitious and smart for her provincial life on Inisherin, but unlike Colm her ambitions are modest and achievable, and in the end she's the only one who escapes a tragic fate. 

Dominic, though not the total fool he initially appears to be, similarly sets his sights too high, and unlike Colm he never even stood a snowball's hell in chance of achieving his goal (being with Siobhan), in the end fully succumbing to his despair.

Only the sweet but simple-minded Padriac is fully content with his life and how things are. But the tragedy of it all is that change is inevitable, and things never stay the way they are forever. Ultimately, whether we're happy with the present or looking longingly towards the future, life has a way of getting in the way of we want. All we can do is be kind to each other. Despite what Colm says, we do remember people for being nice; they may not always go down in the history books, but your legacy isn't just all the achievements you accomplished, but your impact and influence on the people in your life.

Interesting take!

I viewed it as an exercise in the end of friendship. That person from work, that family member, that friend you are just tired of. I had a friend from college, I'll make up a name, let’s call her Rachel Harmafuck. Once she started cheating on Brad with Andrew, then invited Andrew to the engagement party and destination wedding, and wanted me to room him, I was done.

I take a much more humanistic perspective towards BOI. The desire to cut off a toxic friend, and the symbolism of cutting off your fingers, destroying your joy in order to show your staunch position on the matter. I would rather make myself unable to play my instrument, than spend another minute with you. BOI was cathartic for me after what Rachel Harmatuk did, cheating, then inviting Andrew to everything but forcing us all to never tell and to act like everything was normal. I view BOI as a study in cutting off a friend.

Man I love this perspective as well as the comments here too! I have to say when I watched it I loved the film but was so sad and couldn’t understand why the guy was so intent on getting rid of his friend. It did feel pretty cruel in an island where not much happens and where the townsfolk kinda like the routine of their simple lives. 
But these perspectives make me wanna watch it again- especially the Irish civil war take. That honestly never even came up in my mind. 
Great stuff here.

This is my favorite movie of all time, and when people ask me why, I never know how to put it into words. I appreciate any discussion on the film.

Everything is just so perfect to me. The script is good enough to read on its own. The acting is incredible. The allegory is poignant. The costumes, staging, and cinematography are beautiful. I absolutely love the score, so simple yet eerie. 

I could watch this a million times and not be tired of it. Still, I understand why most of my friends find it to be boring.

What's nteresting to me as how Colm and Siobhan are both painted the same, as "thinkers", people looking for their own peace, for the independent break from the humdrumness of being. 
But every move Siobhan makes in pursuit of this is done with love, care and sensitivity (letting Dominc down easy, leaving the island etc.) She engages with art (reading) as a way of connecting with the human experience, even reading "the sad ones."

Colm, in contrast, engages with his art only as an ego-laden idea of legacy and with people only when they can offer him something. He can't tell Padriac why he stopped talking to him and when he does, it isnt done with any kindness or empathy. It's done with cruelty, even if unintentional, because Colm cannot see past himself. Even in his kindest moments, he still pulls himself back from any real emotion or humanness, jumping off the cart the moment Padriac begins to cry, for example. When he tells Padraic nobody has ever been remembered for their kindness, there is a clear view of a portrait of Jesus hanging nearby further highlighting this theme and Colm's harmful misbelief.

Both Siobhan and Colm leave pain and hurt in their development, as inevitably must happen when pursuing one's own needs. But Siobhan who acts with care and kindness only leaves sadness and grief in her wake and ultimately can leave the island with peace. Colm, in contrast, slices off his fingers and robs himself of his own potential legacy because of his anger and spite, and in doing so, he leaves behind meanness and cruelty, which is what winds up being his real legacy (and is also why the title of the film is also the title of Colm's legacy)

The civil war was not a senseless war and was certainly not meaningless. Disagree with whatever side, or with particular actions of each side all you like, but to claim that these were irrational people fighting for the sake of it infantilises and obfuscates the reality that it was a war fought over very serious political and social issues by serious and dedicated people.

Agreed - also to say the two sides were totally "interchangeable" is very ill informed. I personally really disliked the film for many reasons but one was McDonagh trying to shove a Civil War allegory into the broken friendship without any actual historical comparisons with the characters. I can't imagine a director getting away with such trite laziness using any other 20th century conflict.
